summary: "Juvenilia" by Larin-Kyösti is a collection of autobiographical sketches written in the early 20th century. The work evokes a poet’s boyhood in a Finnish town, blending lyrical nature writing with candid portraits of family, servants, neighbors, and youthful exploits. Its central figure is a sensitive, imaginative child whose encounters with loyalty, vice, danger, and beauty shape a nascent artistic conscience. The opening of the collection recalls the narrator reading on a rooftop, lost in Robinson Crusoe, and looking down on his home, yard, park, and neighbors (even glimpsing a young Jean Sibelius), before descending to everyday life. It then paints a warm, wry portrait of Renki-Kustaa, a faithful yet drink-prone farmhand who repeatedly strays and returns, followed by a harsher sketch of a sly gambler whose cheating and influence help unravel the household before his own fortunes collapse. At the start of the long sailing vignette, the boy receives a small boat, learns to handle wind and water, survives a sudden squall, revels in midsummer lights and fireworks, and witnesses both rescues and unsettling signs of death—moments that pierce his innocence while sharpening his sense of the world.
